519.title: Before creation
519.hook: when no form was seen, no sin or virtue, no sun or moon, He alone was (Sukhmani 21)
519.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's twenty-first ashtpadi hear a series of when-questions about the time before creation, each answered by the One alone.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sunn, the stillness, and your line: when there was nothing. Did you let one silence be full instead of awkward? Today the twenty-first ashtpadi asks a string of questions about that stillness. Day five hundred nineteen.

Children are very good at one kind of question. Where was I before I was born? What was there before the house? Before the town? Before the world? Each answer just moves the question back a step, until a parent says, gently, that's enough for tonight. The first stanza of Sukhmani's twenty-first ashtpadi asks those child's questions on purpose, one after another, and it doesn't send anyone to bed. It walks them all the way back, to before creation.
screen: `WHERE WAS I BEFORE I WAS BORN?` → `BEFORE THE TOWN? BEFORE THE WORLD?` → `ALL THE WAY BACK.`

segments.voice: The stanza is built from questions, each beginning jab, when. In paraphrase: when there was no form to be seen, where would sin or virtue have come from? When He was absorbed in the stillness, against whom could anyone hold a grudge? When there was no color or mark, who could feel joy or sorrow? When there was only the Supreme, by Himself, who could be caught in attachment or doubt? And then the closing line: He set His own play in motion, and Nanak says, there is no other maker. Notice what the questions do. They take the things that fill an ordinary day, being right and wrong, grudges, happiness, grief, worry, and quietly show that none of them are the floor of reality. Before them, under them, there was the One. Guru Nanak paints the same scene in raag Maru, with no day or night, no moon or sun: only the One, in stillness. The word for form here is akaar, shape, outline, something you can see. Before creation there was no akaar at all. It's important what the stanza doesn't say. It doesn't say your joys and sorrows are fake. They're real; they belong to the play. It says they aren't the deepest thing. And there's a strange comfort in that. Whatever you're carrying this week, the grudge or the worry, there was a time before it, and Sukhmani says the One who was there then is here now.
screen: `JAB: A STRING OF WHEN QUESTIONS.` · `NO FORM, NO GRUDGE, NO SORROW.` · `AKAAR: NO SHAPE YET.` · `REAL, BUT NOT THE FLOOR.` · then, large: `HE ALONE WAS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: imagine before the first light. Close your eyes. Picture the room fading: the furniture, then the walls. Then the street, the city, the earth, the sun. Let each go, gently, like lights going out one at a time. Rest there, in the dark and the quiet, before anything. Then, slowly, let things return. Notice what's still here. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru in the stillness. The bell holds the time.
Before creation. Sukhmani asks: with no form yet, no grudge or sorrow, what was there? Its answer: the One alone, setting the play in motion.
Your line: he alone was. Today, when a worry grips you, ask the stanza's question: what was here before this? Then breathe once. Day five hundred nineteen.

they're real and belong to the play; they're just not the deepest thing.
the stanza is built from a string of questions
each begins jab, when, and walks back to before creation.
the stanza names a helper who made the world with God

fork.setup: the stanza asks: before any form, when there was only the One, who could hold a grudge? what's the answer it points to?
options: no one: there was only the One.
fork.reveal: no one. with no form and no other, there was nothing to quarrel with. the One alone was, and set the play in motion.

trapdoor: what you thought: before creation is a science question about the start of the universe.
what it means: a string of questions that walks back past sin, grudges and sorrow to the One alone.
what a scholar hears: the stanza's repeated jab-tab, when-then, pattern echoes Guru Nanak's creation hymn in raag Maru, with no day, night, moon or sun.

520.title: Creation begins
520.hook: by His will the play begins (Sukhmani 21)
520.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's twenty-first ashtpadi hear creation begin by God's hukam, as God's own play, after the stillness of sunn.

segments.voice: Yesterday, before creation, and your line: he alone was. When a worry came, did you ask what was there before it? The stillness has lasted two days. Today, something moves. Day five hundred twenty.

A blank document, and a cursor blinking. Blink. Blink. Anyone who has ever had to write something knows that cursor. Everything you could say is still possible, and nothing has been said. Then you type the first word, and suddenly there's a direction, a voice, a shape. The page will never be blank in quite the same way again. After two days of stillness, the twenty-first ashtpadi reaches its first word. Creation begins.
screen: `THE CURSOR BLINKING.` → `THE FIRST WORD TYPED.` → `CREATION BEGINS.`

segments.voice: The stanzas of the twenty-first ashtpadi keep asking what was there before, and then, near the end, the scene changes. In paraphrase: when He Himself fashioned the world of forms, He spread it out through the three qualities; then sin and virtue came to be spoken of, some went to hell and some longed for heaven. Here's the shape of it. First the stillness, sunn. Then, by God's own choice, forms. And only then all the things that fill our lives: right and wrong, reward and loss, hope and fear. They arrive with the world, not before it. The three qualities, the trigun, are an old Indian idea that Gurbani uses often: everything made is woven from three strands, roughly calm, restless and heavy. Gurbani treats them as part of the made world, which God stands beyond. What sets it all going? Sikh teaching answers with one word: hukam, God's will or order. Guru Nanak says in Japji, in paraphrase: by His hukam forms are created; the hukam can't be described. And the picture Sukhmani keeps returning to is a play, khel. God sets His own khel in motion, and is in it. That word matters. A play isn't a machine, ground out because it must be. It's something made freely, with delight. Sikh teaching doesn't say why God began the play, beyond that it was God's will. It leaves the why with the One who began it.
screen: `FIRST THE STILLNESS, THEN FORMS.` · `RIGHT AND WRONG ARRIVE WITH THE WORLD.` · `HUKAM: BY HIS WILL.` · `KHEL: MADE FREELY, LIKE A PLAY.` · then, large: `THE PLAY BEGINS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: begin something small. Sit for a moment in stillness first, the way the ashtpadi did. Then choose one tiny beginning you can make right now: the first sentence of a letter, the first stretch of a walk, the first step of a recipe, one line in a notebook. Make it. Notice the shift from nothing to something, and that you didn't need to know the ending to start. If you pray, you can begin with Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Creation begins. By God's hukam the stillness gives way to forms, and the world, with all its right and wrong, starts as God's own play, khel.
Your line: the play begins. Today, start the thing you've been putting off with just its first small step, and let it be a beginning. Day five hundred twenty.

pairs: the three qualities of the made world

fork.reveal: hukam. Japji says forms are made by His hukam, and the hukam can't be described. Sukhmani calls the result God's own khel, play.

what a scholar hears: Sukhmani places sin, virtue, heaven and hell inside the three-stranded made world, the trigun, which God stands beyond.

sources.ref: Sukhmani Sahib, ashtpadi 21 (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 290–291)

521.title: Living ashtpadi 21
521.hook: the vast and the quiet behind all things
521.tomorrow: Ashtpadi 22, salok: Lord of all beings
521.howItsDone: Many Sikhs rise at amrit vela, the hours before dawn that Japji names as the time to reflect on the Name, and sit in quiet remembrance before the day begins.

segments.voice: Yesterday, creation begins, and your line: the play begins. Did you make the first small start on something? Today we take the twenty-first ashtpadi, the stillness and the beginning, out into an ordinary morning. Day five hundred twenty-one.

If you've ever been awake right before dawn, you know the sky does something odd. It isn't dark and it isn't light. It goes a deep, even gray-blue, and everything is very quiet: no birds yet, no traffic, the trees just shapes. Then, slowly, color comes in from one edge. First a line of pale yellow. Then pink. Then, all at once, it's morning, and the noise of the day begins. The twenty-first ashtpadi happens every dawn, if you know where to look.
screen: `THE GRAY-BLUE BEFORE DAWN.` → `A LINE OF PALE YELLOW.` → `EVERY DAWN, THE ASHTPADI.`

segments.voice: Here's the twenty-first ashtpadi in brief. Before anything, the Formless One, nirankaar, rested in sunn, the deep stillness. There was no form, no grudge, no joy or sorrow, only the One. Then, by God's own will, the play began, and the world of forms spread out. Living that doesn't mean thinking about the beginning of the universe all day. It means remembering that the stillness didn't go anywhere. In Sikh teaching, the One who rested in sunn is the same One inside the play now, behind all things, the way the quiet gray sky is still there behind the colors of the sunrise. That's why so many Sikhs value amrit vela, the hours before dawn. In Japji, Guru Nanak names that ambrosial hour as the time to reflect on the greatness of the Name. It's the time of day that looks most like the ashtpadi: quiet first, then the world. Sitting with the Name then is a way of meeting the stillness before the noise begins, so that you can carry a little of it into the noise. And the noise is not the enemy. Sikh teaching has no quarrel with the busy day; the Gurus worked, farmed, traded and led. The point is that behind the busyness there's something vast and quiet that the busyness can't touch. Some days you feel it. Some days you don't. Sukhmani says it's there either way.
screen: `STILLNESS, THEN THE PLAY.` · `THE STILLNESS DIDN'T GO ANYWHERE.` · `AMRIT VELA: QUIET FIRST.` · `THE BUSY DAY IS NOT THE ENEMY.` · then, large: `BEHIND ALL THINGS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch the dawn. If it's early, go to a window and watch the sky change. If it isn't, close your eyes and remember a dawn you've seen, or look at whatever sky is outside now. Watch slowly. Notice the quiet underneath the color, or underneath the light and noise of the day. Let your breath be as slow as the sky. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru, behind all things. The bell holds the time.
Living ashtpadi 21. The stillness God rested in before creation is still here, behind the play; amrit vela, before dawn, is a daily way to meet it.
Your line: behind all things. Tomorrow, try waking ten minutes earlier and sit before the day's noise starts. Tonight, set the alarm. Day five hundred twenty-one.

screen: `DAY 521 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: ASHTPADI 22, SALOK: LORD OF ALL BEINGS.`

522.title: Ashtpadi 22, salok: Lord of all beings
522.hook: jeea jant ke thaakuraa: Lord of all beings, pervading all (Sukhmani 22)
522.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's twenty-second ashtpadi begin with a salok naming God the Master of all living beings, the One spread through every creature.

segments.voice: Yesterday, living ashtpadi 21, and your line: behind all things. Did you catch a little quiet before the day's noise? The twenty-first ashtpadi brought the world into being. The twenty-second looks at who lives in it. Day five hundred twenty-two.

A single ant on the kitchen counter, walking a careful line toward a grain of sugar. Most of us have a reflex for that moment: a paper towel, a thumb. But if you stop and actually watch it, it's remarkable. It's carrying something heavier than itself. It's checking the way with its antennae. It's going somewhere, for some reason that matters to it. The twenty-second ashtpadi of Sukhmani opens by naming the Lord of that ant, and of everything else that breathes.
screen: `ONE ANT ON THE COUNTER.` → `IT'S GOING SOMEWHERE.` → `THE LORD OF EVERYTHING THAT BREATHES.`

segments.voice: The salok, in paraphrase: Lord and Master of all beings and creatures, You Yourself are present in all of them. Nanak says: the One is spread out everywhere; where could a second be seen? Start with jeea jant. Jeea are living beings, things with life and breath. Jant are creatures, every kind of animal. Together the phrase is Gurbani's way of saying everyone and everything alive: people, ants, birds, fish, the cat on the windowsill. Thaakur is lord or master, a word of respect for the one in charge of a household or estate. So the salok begins: Master of every living thing. But the second half changes what master means. God isn't pictured as a landlord far off, collecting rent. Aape vartanhaar: God Himself is the one moving within them all, present and active in each. And then the last line: eko pasariaa. The One has spread out. Where is there a second to see? This is why Sikh teaching speaks so warmly about all living things. If the same One is spread through every creature, then the ant on the counter isn't simply a pest or a stranger. It's kin, in a real sense: made by the same Master, filled by the same presence. That doesn't mean Sikhs never swat a mosquito. It means the glance you give a living thing can carry a little respect. Today's ashtpadi begins by widening the circle of who counts.
screen: `JEEA JANT: EVERYTHING ALIVE.` · `THAAKUR: LORD AND MASTER.` · `NOT FAR OFF: MOVING WITHIN.` · `EKO PASARIAA: THE ONE, SPREAD OUT.` · then, large: `LORD OF ALL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: feel kin to a creature. Find a living thing you can see or hear: a bird outside, a houseplant, a pet, a fly on the window, even a picture of an animal you love. Watch it for a while. Notice its breathing, its movement, the way it pays attention to its world. Then quietly hold the thought: the same Master, the same life. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru as you watch. The bell holds the time.
Ashtpadi 22. Its salok calls God thaakur of jeea jant, Master of every living thing, and says the One is spread through them all.
Your line: lord of all. Today, when you meet an insect indoors, try carrying it outside instead. Day five hundred twenty-two.

523.title: In every heart
523.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's twenty-second ashtpadi hear that God dwells ghat ghat, in every heart, a teaching lived out in langar's shared rows and in seva to all.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ashtpadi 22, and your line: lord of all. Did an insect get a ride outside instead of a paper towel? Yesterday the circle widened to every living thing. Today it moves inward, to the heart. Day five hundred twenty-three.

A subway car at rush hour. Forty strangers, shoulder to shoulder, all carefully not looking at one another. A man in a suit reading his phone. A teenager with headphones and eyes closed. A grandmother with grocery bags, a nurse just off a night shift. Each face closed, like a house with the curtains drawn. You could ride with them every day for a year and never know one name. The twenty-second ashtpadi makes a claim about every one of those closed houses. Someone lives inside.
screen: `FORTY STRANGERS, NOT LOOKING.` → `EACH FACE A CLOSED HOUSE.` → `SOMEONE LIVES INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday's salok said the One is spread through all beings. The twenty-second ashtpadi presses the point home: God dwells in every heart, ghat ghat, in each body and each being. Ghat literally means a pot or vessel, a clay jar. Gurbani uses it for the body, and for the heart inside it, the way a jar holds water. Ghat ghat, doubled, means in every single one. Gurbani returns to this again and again. In the evening prayer, Sohila, Guru Nanak sings, in paraphrase: within all is the Light, and You are that Light; by its shining, everything shines. Every face on that subway car is a clay jar with the same Light inside. This is the ground under some of the most practical things Sikhs do. It's why the langar, the free kitchen, seats everyone on the floor in the same rows, whoever they are. It's why the Gurus spoke so sharply against treating people as high or low by caste. And it's why, for Sikhs, seva, serving others, is never only charity. If the Light is in every heart, then serving a stranger is serving the One who lives there. That's a demanding teaching. It's easy to see the Light in a smiling child, or a kind friend. It's harder in the man who shoved past you to get a seat. Sukhmani doesn't make an exception for him. Ghat ghat means every jar.
screen: `GHAT GHAT: IN EVERY VESSEL.` · `THE SAME LIGHT IN EACH.` · `THE GROUND UNDER LANGAR AND SEVA.` · `NO EXCEPTIONS, EVEN THE RUDE ONE.` · then, large: `EVERY HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for Him in one face. Bring to mind one face, or look at one, a photo or a person nearby. Choose someone ordinary, not your favorite person in the world. Look slowly: the eyes, the lines, the expression. Then hold the thought: there's Light in this jar too. Stay with it as long as you can. If it feels easy, choose a harder face. If you pray, you can say Waheguru softly as you look. The bell holds the time.
In every heart. Ghat ghat: Sukhmani says God dwells in every vessel, every body and heart, and Sohila adds that the same Light shines in all.
Your line: every heart. Today, look one stranger in the eye, a cashier, a driver, someone on the street, and offer a real hello. Day five hundred twenty-three.

524.title: Sustainer of all
524.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib hear that God sustains every creature, and each evening in Rehras recite Guru Arjan's hymn picturing food set out even for creatures within rocks.

segments.voice: Yesterday, in every heart, and your line: every heart. Did you give one stranger a real hello? The twenty-second ashtpadi named the Master of all beings, then found Him inside each one. Today: who feeds them. Day five hundred twenty-four.

Split a rock in a field, and sometimes there's a tiny creature living inside: a beetle in a damp hollow, a grub, a pale little worm. Nobody brings it groceries. Nobody checks on it. And yet there it is, alive, with what it needs. Guru Arjan, the same Guru who wrote Sukhmani, used exactly that picture in a hymn Sikhs recite every evening. And it's the picture under today's line from the twenty-second ashtpadi. Today: the sustainer of all.
screen: `A CREATURE INSIDE A ROCK.` → `NOBODY BRINGS IT GROCERIES.` → `THE SUSTAINER OF ALL.`

segments.voice: The twenty-second ashtpadi, which began by naming God the Master of all beings, says that God sustains each one of them. The word Sikhs often use for that sustenance is rijak: daily bread, livelihood, what keeps a creature alive. Guru Arjan unfolds the idea in a hymn in raag Gujri that's part of Rehras, the evening prayer. In paraphrase: why, mind, do you scheme and worry, when God Himself is busy caring for you? Even in rocks and stones He made creatures, and set their food before them. Then comes a picture many Sikhs love. A migrating crane flies hundreds of miles, leaving her young behind. Who feeds them? Who teaches them to eat? Have you never thought of that? It's a striking image: the chicks alone, the mother far away, and still they're fed. Now, notice what this teaching isn't. It isn't a promise that no one will ever go hungry, and it isn't permission to stop working. Sikhs are taught kirat karni, honest work, and the whole institution of langar exists because people do go hungry, and Sikhs believe feeding them is God's work done through human hands. The point is about worry. Guru Arjan isn't telling the mind to stop trying. He's telling it to stop scheming and fretting as if everything depended on it alone. The rock creature and the crane's chicks are fed. And often, Sikhs would say, the way God feeds someone is through you.
screen: `RIJAK: WHAT KEEPS A CREATURE ALIVE.` · `IN ROCKS AND STONES, FOOD SET OUT.` · `THE CRANE FLIES; THE CHICKS ARE FED.` · `NOT A REASON TO STOP WORKING.` · then, large: `HE FEEDS ALL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: feed a bird or a pet. If you have a pet, give it a little food or fresh water now, slowly, paying attention. If not, put a few crumbs or seeds on a windowsill or balcony. If neither is possible, water a plant. Then sit and breathe. Watch, or picture, the creature receiving it. Notice that for this moment you're part of how it's sustained. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you give. The bell holds the time.
Sustainer of all. Sukhmani says God sustains each creature; Guru Arjan pictures food set out even in rocks, and a crane's chicks fed while she's far away.
Your line: he feeds all. Today, when a money or food worry starts its loop, do one practical thing about it, then let the scheming rest. Day five hundred twenty-four.

525.title: Living ashtpadi 22
525.tomorrow: Ashtpadi 23, salok: the ointment of wisdom
525.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's twenty-second ashtpadi hear that every living being belongs to the One, and Sikh tradition remembers Guru Har Rai for his care of gardens, animals and the sick.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sustainer of all, and your line: he feeds all. A week ends today. It began before creation, he alone was; then the play began, the quiet behind all things, the Lord of all, every heart, and the One who feeds every creature. Today we live it. Day five hundred twenty-five.

Sikhs tell a story about the seventh Guru, Guru Har Rai, when he was a boy. Walking through a garden in a long, flowing robe, he brushed past a flowering bush, and a few petals fell to the ground. His grandfather, Guru Hargobind, saw it and told him gently that a robe that wide must be carried with care. The boy, the story goes, was so moved that he kept that care all his life. Today the twenty-second ashtpadi steps out into the garden.
screen: `A BOY, A ROBE, A FLOWERING BUSH.` → `A FEW PETALS FALL.` → `CARRY IT WITH CARE.`

segments.voice: Here's the twenty-second ashtpadi in brief. God is the thaakur, the Master, of jeea jant, every living being. The One is spread through them all, dwelling ghat ghat, in every heart, and sustaining each creature with its daily bread. Put that together and you get one plain line: everything alive is His. Living it starts with how we touch things. The story of Guru Har Rai is a story people tell, passed down in Sikh tradition rather than recorded in the Guru Granth Sahib. But its point fits the ashtpadi exactly. If every living thing belongs to the One, then a flower isn't just scenery and an animal isn't just a resource. They're in someone else's care, and we're walking through the garden. Sikh tradition remembers Guru Har Rai as a lover of gardens and animals, and as someone who kept medicines to give to the sick, including, by many accounts, the son of the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan, whose family were no friends of the Gurus. That detail matters. Everything alive is His, including the people we'd rather not help. In practice, this can be very small. Watering the office plant that everyone forgets. Driving a little slower past the park. Asking how the elderly neighbor's dog is doing. None of it is grand. But each small act says: this life isn't mine to waste. It belongs to the One who is spread through all.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: care for one living thing. Yesterday was food; today is care. Choose one: a plant that needs water, a bit of litter on the path outside, a tired person in your home who needs a cup of tea. Do it slowly, as if it belonged to someone you love, because in the ashtpadi's picture it does. If there's nothing nearby, sit and picture a living thing you'll care for later today, and plan exactly how. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you tend it. The bell holds the time.
Living ashtpadi 22. Every living being has the same Master, the same indwelling Light, the same Feeder; so every living thing is handled with care.
Your line: everything alive is his. Today, find one neglected living thing, a plant, an animal, a person, and give it a moment of real care. Day five hundred twenty-five.
